subject: deep sea amphipod
title: At the Ocean's Deepest Point, This Animal Makes Armour From Mud

scenes.text: This deep-sea crustacean forges its own aluminium armour.
Hirondellea gigas, a shrimp-like animal about 2 inches long. It lives at the bottom of the Mariana Trench, nearly 11 kilometers down.
The pressure there is over 1,000 times what you feel now. Seawater that deep slowly dissolves shells made of calcium carbonate.
In 2019, Japanese scientists found how it survives. Its body is coated in a gel of aluminium hydroxide.
Its gut pulls aluminium out of swallowed seabed mud. The metal reacts with seawater and sets into a protective film over the shell.
It also eats sunken wood, with digestive enzymes almost no animal has. The deepest scavenger alive built its armour from dirt.

description:
An amphipod at the bottom of the Mariana Trench coats itself in aluminium it extracts from seabed mud.
Hirondellea gigas lives at nearly 11,000 meters, where pressure exceeds 1,000 atmospheres and calcium carbonate shells tend to dissolve. A 2019 study in PLOS ONE found its exoskeleton covered by an aluminium hydroxide gel: the animal takes up aluminium from ingested sediment, and the metal forms a protective layer when it meets seawater. The same species digests sunken wood with its own cellulase enzymes.
Which deep-sea survival trick impresses you most?
first_comment: The same amphipods swarm any bait dropped into the trench within hours. What else do you think is living at the very bottom?
